paper_title: Chaos in the Text: Revealing the Modality Preference in Mixed-Modality Retrievers

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Dense retrievers have made significant progress on text and image corpora, but whether these capabilities extend reliably to mixed corpora containing text, image, and fused text-image documents remains unclear. In this paper, we systematically examine retrievers across architectures and find that their performance is highly sensitive to modality composition. As image documents are progressively replaced with semantically corresponding text representations, retrieval performance follows a pronounced V-shaped curve, remaining strong on single-modality corpora but degrading substantially when modalities coexist. In particular, irrelevant text causes more severe degradation than an equal number of irrelevant images, a phenomenon we term Chaos in the Text. Further analysis reveals modality preference, whereby text representations receive systematically higher similarity scores, allowing irrelevant text to outrank relevant images. To mitigate this bias, we introduce Trident, which constructs text, image, and fused text-image views of each document as co-equal positives and jointly optimizes relevance discrimination and positive-view balance through Multi-Positive View InfoNCE. Experiments across visual document and natural image benchmarks show that trident improves mixed-modality retrieval on both CLIP-based and VLM-based architectures, reduces sensitivity to modality composition and text distractors, and increases average single-modality retrieval performance.

sections.title: ABSTRACT
sections.content: Dense retrievers have made significant progress on text and image corpora, but whether these capabilities extend reliably to mixed corpora containing text, image, and fused text-image documents remains unclear. In this paper, we systematically examine retrievers across architectures and find that their performance is highly sensitive to modality composition. As image documents are progressively replaced with semantically corresponding text representations, retrieval performance follows pronounced V-shaped curve, remaining strong on single-modality corpora but degrading substantially when modalities coexist. In particular, irrelevant text causes more severe degradation than an equal number of irrelevant images, phenomenon we term Chaos in the Text. Further analysis reveals modality preference, whereby text representations receive systematically higher similarity scores, allowing irrelevant text to outrank relevant images. To mitigate this bias, we introduce Trident, which constructs text, image, and fused textimage views of each document as co-equal positives and jointly optimizes relevance discrimination and positive-view balance through Multi-Positive View InfoNCE. Experiments across visual document and natural image benchmarks show that trident improves mixed-modality retrieval on both CLIP-based and VLMbased architectures, reduces sensitivity to modality composition and text distractors, and increases average single-modality retrieval performance.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: In recent years, image retrieval has made significant progress in natural-image (Jia et al., 2021; Li et al., 2025b) and visual-document retrieval (Faysse et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025) by directly encoding images and retrieving relevant content from image corpora. This approach preserves visual information often lost in text conversion and provides relevant evidence (Peng et al., 2026; Tanaka et al., 2025) to support better information gathering in multimodal RAG (Sun et al., 2025; Peng et al., 2025; Xiong et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026). However, real-world corpora often contain mixture of text-only, image-only, and fused text-image documents, with relevant evidence potentially residing in any modality (Wei et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2026), which requires retrievers to compare querydocument relevance across modalities and rank all candidates in unified list. Despite its importance, we find that existing multimodal retrievers are highly sensitive to the modality composition of mixed-modality corpora. As illustrated in Figure 1, progressively replacing documents in an image corpus with their semantically corresponding text representations yields pronounced V-shaped performance curve. Models perform well on purely image or purely text corpora, while degrading substantially when the two modalities coexist. Further inspection reveals that models tend to rank irrelevant text documents above highly relevant image documents, pushing visual evidence containing the answer out of the top-K results. We term this phenomenon Chaos in the Text. These findings indicate that strong retrieval performance on single-modality corpora does not guarantee reliable access to relevant evidence in mixed-modality settings. 1 (a) (b) Figure 1: (a) Retrieval robustness degrades sharply in mixed-modality corpora. As image documents are progressively replaced by text documents, NDCG@10 follows an asymmetric V-shaped curve. (b) Chaos in the Text: text documents are systematically over-ranked regardless of semantic relevance, pushing key documents out of the top-K when the answer resides in the image modality. To investigate the cause of this phenomenon, we further analyze similarity distributions across document modalities. Specifically, we construct three semantically corresponding representations for each document: text, image, and fused text-image, and compare their similarities to the same set of queries. We find that multiple retrievers systematically assign higher similarity scores to text representations than to image representations, even when considering only positive querydocument pairs. This indicates that retrieval scores reflect not only semantic relevance but also systematic influence of document modality, revealing Modality Preference. When documents of different modalities compete in the same candidate pool, this bias translates into ranking advantage, allowing irrelevant text documents to outrank relevant image documents. To alleviate this phenomenon, we introduce Trident, contrastive learning framework that balances modalities through multiple positive views. Specifically, Trident constructs text, image, and fused text-image representations of each document as three co-equal positives for the same query and jointly optimizes them with Multi-Positive InfoNCE objective under shared normalization. While separating relevant documents from irrelevant ones, this objective discourages positive probability mass from concentrating on single modality, encouraging the model to account for relevant evidence across modalities and thereby mitigating modality preference in mixed-modality retrieval. Extensive experiments show that trident substantially mitigates the modality preference while improving overall retrieval performance. After trident training, models exhibit more stable retrieval performance on mixed-modality corpora, with reduced sensitivity to modality proportions and text distractors, while also achieving higher average retrieval performance on the original singlemodality corpora. These improvements hold across both CLIP-based and VLM-based retrieval architectures, demonstrating the effectiveness and broad applicability of our training approach.

sections.title: 2 HOW RETRIEVAL MODELS PERFORM ON MIXED-MODALITY CORPORA?
sections.content: Although multimodal retrieval models perform strongly on single-modality corpora (text-only or image-only), real-world corpora, as discussed in Section 1, typically mix text, image, and textimage fused documents. How reliably models retrieve from such mixed-modality corpora, however, has not been systematically quantified. We therefore examine retrieval performance in this setting. 2.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP AND MODELS Task formulation and metric. This requires relevance scores to be comparable across modalities within unified ranking. Each query may have one or more relevant documents. Following common practice (Muennighoff et al., 2023; Meng et al., 2025), we adopt NDCG@10 as our primary metric. (2) Benchmarks and mixed-modality corpus construction. We evaluate on ChartQA (Masry et al., 2022) and SlideVQA (Tanaka et al., 2023), following the modality-replacement protocol of Li et al. (2025a). For each image document, we use Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B-Instruct (Team, 2025) to generate detailed description and brief summary. The description forms the Text view, the original image forms the Image view, and the summary paired with the image forms the Fused view. Given target proportions of the three modalities, we independently sample one view per document according to these proportions. This preserves document identities and corpus size while varying the modality composition. Models. V-shaped performance under modality mixing. As shown in Figure 2, both CLIP-based and VLM-based visual retrievers exhibit similar V-shaped performance curves on the two benchmarks. Starting from an image-only corpus, retrieval performance drops markedly as image documents are progressively replaced with semantically corresponding text representations, reaches trough when the two modalities are mixed, and then recovers as the text proportion increases and the corpus approaches text-only composition. This indicates that models perform well on purely image or purely text corpora but struggle to maintain stable retrieval performance when the two coexist. In contrast, increasing the proportion of fused text-image documents does not induce similar Vshaped degradation and instead alleviates the performance drop caused by mixing text and image documents. This contrast highlights the degradation arising from the coexistence of text-only and image-only documents as prominent challenge in mixed-modality retrieval. Specifically, we start with each benchmarks original image-only corpus, separately add irrelevant text passages and images sampled from the Wikipedia corpus (Sun et al., 2026), and track retrieval performance as the number of distractors increases. We find that, with the same number of distractors, irrelevant images have relatively modest effect on retrieval performance, whereas irrelevant text causes sharp decline. This difference persists across models and benchmarks, indicating that candidate-pool expansion alone cannot explain the degradation. We term this substantial deterioration in retrieval performance caused by introducing irrelevant text into an image corpus Chaos in the Text. This phenomenon further suggests that models may exhibit systematic scoring biases across document modalities, allowing modality to influence rankings that should be determined by semantic relevance.

sections.title: 3 WHY DO RETRIEVAL MODELS EXHIBIT CHAOS IN THE TEXT?
sections.content: Given that Chaos in the Text is consistently observed across different models and benchmarks, its underlying cause remains unclear. We hypothesize that retrieval models may not rank documents purely by semantic relevance, but instead exhibit an inherent bias toward text documents. To test this, we construct three semantically identical, modality-distinct corpora (pure text, pure image, and text-image fused) and issue the same queries against each, comparing the resulting similarity distributions to examine whether modality itself systematically influences ranking. 1Results for the remaining models are shown in Appendix A. 4 Figure 4: (a) Violin plots show the similarity distributions across document modalities, revealing systematically higher similarity for text documents. (b) Each dot compares querys positive similarity with its text hard-negative similarity; points above y=x indicate cases where an irrelevant text document outranks the positive document, with the interference rate reporting their fraction. 3.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP We reuse the SlideVQA benchmark, retrieval models, and the three semantically aligned, modalitydistinct parallel corpora (text, image, fused) from Section 2.1. For each corpus, we compute cosine similarities between the same query set and its documents, yielding similarity distribution per (query, doc modality) combination. We report two statistics: the all-pair mean, averaged over all query-document pairs, characterizing the overall similarity level of that modality; and the positivepair mean, averaged only over ground-truth relevant pairs annotated in the qrels, characterizing the similarity score when relevance genuinely holds. systematic discrepancy in these means across the three corpora would indicate that retrieval ranking is not governed purely by semantic relevance, but is confounded by modality itself. 3.2 RESULTS AND DISCUSSION We analyze modality preference from two perspectives, examining cross-modal similarity differences among relevant documents and ranking interference from irrelevant text. Cross-Modal Score Differences among Relevant Documents. As shown in Figure 4(a), all three models exhibit similar score disparities for the same queries and their semantically corresponding relevant documents. The mean similarity between text queries and text positives is higher than that for image and fused text-image positives, with image positives showing the largest gap. Although the fused view narrows this gap, its similarity remains below that of the text view. This indicates that even when documents are relevant to the query, models assign different scores depending on their modality. The consistent trend across CLIP-based retrievers and VLM-based retrievers of different scales suggests that this modality preference is not specific to particular architecture or model size. 5 Figure 5: Overview of Trident. Left: for each document, we construct tri-modal positive views (text, image, and fused), and all other views in the batch serve as negatives. The three positives and the negatives are jointly normalized by shared softmax. Right: Multi-Positive View InfoNCE decomposes into relevance discrimination, which increases the total positive probability mass, and positive-view balance, which prevents the mass from being dominated by single modality. Ranking Interference from Irrelevant Text. To examine whether these score differences affect the ranking of relevant and irrelevant documents, Figure 4(b) compares each querys similarity to its relevant document and text hard negative. Each point represents query, with positive similarity on the horizontal axis and text hard-negative similarity on the vertical axis. Points above the diagonal therefore indicate that irrelevant text receives higher score than the relevant document. When the relevant document is presented as an image, most queries lie above the diagonal across all three models, indicating that irrelevant text frequently outscores genuinely relevant images. This interference is substantially reduced when the relevant document is presented as text. Fused views alleviate interference to some extent, but considerable proportion of queries remain affected, with varying improvements across models. These comparisons show that modality preference extends beyond differences in mean similarity to directly disrupt relevance-based ranking. The scoring advantage of text can outweigh the semantic relevance of image documents.

sections.title: 4 HOW CAN WE MITIGATE MODALITY PREFERENCE?
sections.content: To alleviate the modality preference and promote joint learning across modalities, we introduce trident, contrastive learning framework based on multiple positive views. Trident constructs text, image, and fused text-image views as three co-equal positives for the same query and jointly optimizes them within shared candidate space. This enables relevant evidence across modalities to contribute to retrieval learning while reducing the influence of modality preference on ranking. 4.1 TRIDENT We introduce trident through modality-balanced data construction and joint optimization of multiple positive views. Modality-balanced data construction. To mitigate modality preference when matching queries with documents, we introduce Modality-Balanced Data Construction, which provides each query with multiple positive views across modalities. Existing training data typically pairs query with relevant document in single modality, offering limited comparable supervision across modalities for the same query. We extend this single-positive pairing into three-view pairing, enabling the model to jointly learn the relevance of different modality representations of the same document. Specifically, we use Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B-Instruct to generate detailed textual description and concise summary for each image document. The detailed description forms the Text view, the original image forms the Image view, and the summary paired with the original image forms the Fused view. All three views serve as positives for the corresponding query, providing modalitybalanced supervision for joint optimization. 6 Multi-positive view InfoNCE. sections.title: 5 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Multimodal retrieval models. Dense multimodal retrieval was established by dual-tower contrastive encoders such as CLIP (Radford et al., 2021), ALIGN (Jia et al., 2021), and their successors SigLIP/SigLIP 2 (Zhai et al., 2023; Tschannen et al., 2025), which align text and images in shared space but encode each modality through separate tower. Research subsequently shifted toward vision-language model (VLM) backbones that ingest interleaved text and image tokens in single transformer and emit one unified embedding, including VLM2Vec and VLM2Vec-V2 (Jiang et al., 2024; Meng et al., 2025), GME (Zhang et al., 2024), UniME (Gu et al., 2025), and Qwen3-VLEmbedding (Li et al., 2026), which now dominate universal-embedding leaderboards. However, these systems, together with the standard benchmarks used to evaluate them, such as BEIR (Thakur et al., 2021), MTEB (Muennighoff et al., 2023), and the document VQA datasets we adopt, are almost entirely built on single-modality corpora, and therefore cannot assess how multimodal retrieval models perform when retrieving over mixed-modality corpus. Modality gap. Prior work has shown that contrastive vision-language embeddings are not modalityagnostic. Liang et al. (2022) first noted the modality gap, in which image and text embeddings occupy disjoint cones of the hypersphere, an artifact of initialization and the contrastive temperature (Shi et al., 2023); later work attributes this to information imbalance across modalities (Schrodi et al., 2025; Fahim et al., 2024) and attempts to close it via geometric interventions such as manifold mixup (Oh et al., 2023; Eslami & De Melo, 2024). Yet these studies measure the gap purely geometrically and evaluate it on cross-modal alignment tasks, where uniform offset between the two clusters is harmless, since all candidates share modality and the offset cancels out in ranking. We find, however, that in mixed-modality retrieval, what corrupts the ranking is not the geometric modality gap, but modality preference internal to the model.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: In this paper, we reveal the sensitivity of multimodal retrieval models to corpus modality composition and identifies Chaos in the Text, phenomenon in which introducing irrelevant text into an image corpus substantially degrades retrieval performance. Further analysis reveals sys9 tematic biases in similarity scores across modalities, compromising the comparability of candidate documents. To mitigate this issue, we introduce trident, which combines modality-balanced data construction with Multi-Positive View InfoNCE to jointly promote relevance discrimination and positive-view balance. Experiments on CLIP-based and VLM-based architectures show that trident improves mixed-modality retrieval, reduces sensitivity to modality proportions, and increases average single-modality retrieval performance.

The results show that the sensitivity of retrieval performance to the proportion of text, image, and fused documents in the corpus is not an idiosyncrasy of the representative models discussed above, but deficiency shared by nearly all evaluated retrieval models. With the exception of the GR-CLIPbased subfigures, the remaining models exhibit the same asymmetric V-shaped surface observed in the main text on both benchmarks: as the corpus transitions from purely image documents toward an increasing proportion of text, NDCG@10 first drops markedly, reaching its minimum around some intermediate ratio, before recovering as the text ratio continues to increase toward purely text corpus. Notably, SigLIP2-L/16-384 and VisRAG-Ret exhibit sharp, localized peaks near the boundaries of the surface (i.e., where one modalitys proportion approaches one), indicating that these models achieve their best performance only when the corpus is composed of single modality (purely text or purely image); performance drops sharply as soon as even small proportion of another modality is introduced. This suggests that such models rely heavily on the modality purity of the corpus, rather than exhibiting genuine adaptability to mixed-modality settings. In contrast, even GR-CLIP, post-hoc correction method specifically designed to address mixedmodality retrieval for CLIP-based models, fails to fully resolve this robustness deficiency. As shown in subfigures (d)(f), applying GR-CLIP correction narrows the overall range of performance fluctuation and reduces the absolute magnitude of degradation relative to the uncorrected models; however, the underlying V-shaped degradation pattern persists-performance still varies systematically with the proportion of text, image, and fused documents in the corpus, rather than being flattened into stable surface. More importantly, GR-CLIPs correction depends on pre-computing modalitywise statistics over large domain-specific reference corpus, requirement that inherently limits its transferability and practicality in open-domain settings or under unknown corpus distributions. This indicates that even targeted post-hoc correction method can only partially mitigate, rather than eliminate, the sensitivity of multimodal retrieval models to the modality proportions of the corpus. Taken together, the complete results for all nine models on both benchmarks further reinforce the core conclusion of the main text: regardless of architecture, scale, training paradigm, or the use of targeted post-hoc correction, current mainstream multimodal retrieval models generally lack robustness to variation in the proportion of text, image, and fused documents in the corpus. Following the same protocol as in the main text, we examine modality preference from two perspectives: (i) score differences among semantically corresponding positive documents presented in different modalities, and (ii) ranking interference caused by irrelevant text documents. The additional results cover broader set of CLIP-based retrievers and recent multimodal embedding models. Additional CLIP-based retrievers. Figure 11 extends the analysis to CLIP-ViT-L/14, SigLIP2L, and AltCLIP, together with their GR-CLIP-corrected counterparts. The positive-pair distributions in Figure 11(a) reproduce the modality-dependent score differences observed in the main text. In particular, the similarity assigned to an image positive is substantially lower than that assigned to its semantically corresponding text positive for CLIP-ViT-L/14, SigLIP2-L, and AltCLIP. More importantly, the same asymmetry appears at the ranking level in Figure 11(b). When the relevant document is presented as an image, text hard negatives frequently receive higher similarity scores than the positive, producing high interference rates across the three retrievers. The effect is particularly pronounced for CLIP-ViT-L/14 and SigLIP2-L, where nearly all image-positive queries in our sample are affected. In contrast, interference is generally lower when the positive itself is presented as text. These results further support that modality preference is not merely shift in average similarity, but can directly alter the ranking between relevant and irrelevant documents. The GR-CLIP variants provide an additional comparison. Although post-hoc correction can reduce the positive-score gap for some models, the ranking-level behavior is not consistently resolved. For example, substantial text-negative interference remains for image positives after correction, and the effect varies considerably across backbone models and positive modalities. This suggests that calibrating the similarity space alone does not necessarily remove the underlying modality-dependent ranking behavior. Other VLM-based retrievers and Trident. sections.title: F MODEL PERFORMANCE ON NATURAL IMAGES
sections.content: Experimental Setup. To verify that our findings extend to natural images, we train on 170K samples collected from the training sets of MMEB (Jiang et al., 2024), and evaluate on four natural-image retrieval benchmarks: Google-WIT (Srinivasan et al., 2021), MSCOCO (Chen et al., 2015), VisualNews (Liu et al., 2021), and OVEN (Hu et al., 2023)  (Table 4)  . Origin denotes each datasets original single-modality corpus, while Mix directly adopts the mixed-modality corpus from MixBench (Li et al., 2025a), which merges the four datasets. Existing models remain non-robust in mixed-modality retrieval on natural images. Most baselines degrade substantially from Origin to Mix: average NDCG@10 drops from 53.13 to 21.81 for SigLIP2, from 69.32 to 37.98 for CLIP-ViT-L/14, and from 55.67 to 33.91 for VisRAG-Ret. Meanwhile, some models, including Trident, score higher in Mix than in Origin (e.g., Qwen3-VLEmbedding-2B rises from 66.60 to 73.67). This contrasts with document images: document images contain abundant text and thus align readily with textual semantics, whereas natural-image semantics are sparser and more abstract, making them harder to match with text queries, while the semantically equivalent text documents substituted in Mix are explicit and easier to retrieve. The Origin-to-Mix change on natural images therefore conflates dataset characteristics with robustness, and is better judged by comparing models on the same Mix corpus. 24 By mitigating modality preference, Trident remains effective on natural images. On the same Mix corpus, Trident, which trains toward modality balance, achieves the highest Mix average on both backbones (70.50 and 76.78), clearly surpassing the corresponding baselines Jina-CLIP-v2 (56.43) and Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B (73.67), while its Origin average does not decrease. This shows that mitigating modality preference does not compromise single-modality retrieval. Consistent with the main text, removing Multi-Positive InfoNCE lowers the Mix average on both backbones, confirming that an objective that balances modalities during training is effective.

sections.title: G FURTHER ABLATION STUDIES
sections.content: We further examine how the two components of Trident contribute to mitigating modality preference. As shown in Figure 14, the original Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B exhibits substantial disparity across sameand cross-modality positive pairs, with standard deviation of σ = 0.055 across the six group means. Training with our modality-balanced data construction alone (w/o Multi-Positive InfoNCE) reduces σ to 0.009, indicating that balanced positive sampling already alleviates modalitydependent disparity. Incorporating Multi-Positive InfoNCE further reduces σ to 0.004, consistent with the positive-view balancing effect characterized by Eq. 6: the shared softmax discourages the positive probability mass from being systematically concentrated in single modality. Together with the retrieval gains in Table 1, these results show that data-level balance and objective-level coordination provide complementary contributions to mitigating modality preference. natural question is whether stronger modality balancing would further improve retrieval. To test this, we augment Multi-Positive InfoNCE with an explicit Modality Balance Loss that directly penalizes similarity differences among the three positive views, and compare = 200 with the default = 0. As shown in Figure 15(a), both settings exhibit similar convergence of the retrieval objective. More importantly, the balance loss decreases rapidly even when it is not explicitly optimized (w = 0; Figure 15(b)), providing additional empirical evidence that Multi-Positive InfoNCE already reduces modality disparity through its shared objective. Explicit balancing pushes this effect further, reducing σ from 0.004 to 0.003 in Figure 14. However, this lower disparity does not yield better retrieval: although = 200 performs slightly better early in training, its advantage disappears and the final NDCG@10 is slightly lower than that of = 0 (Figure 15(c)). This result reveals an important distinction between mitigating modality preference and enforcing similarity equality. The positive-view balance induced by Multi-Positive InfoNCE operates on the relative probability mass within the shared softmax, discouraging systematic dominance by any single modality without directly requiring their cosine similarities to be identical. In contrast, the additional Modality Balance Loss explicitly pushes the similarities of Text, Image, and Fused views toward equality. Such constraint can be overly restrictive because these views differ inherently in information content and granularity; for example, an image may contain visual evidence that is not fully captured by its textual description. Their optimal similarities to query therefore need not coincide. The slightly better retrieval performance of = 0, despite its marginally larger similarity dispersion (0.004 vs. 0.003), supports this distinction. Modality balance does not require different modalities to have identical similarities; rather, it requires preventing any single modality from systematically dominating the shared representation space. FULL 3D SURFACE COMPARISONS BEFORE AND AFTER TRIDENT To further validate the robustness of Trident beyond the two datasets presented in the main text, we extend the 3D surface analysis to four additional benchmarks: ChartQA, InfoVQA, DocVQA, and ViDoSeek. Figure 16 reports Mean NDCG@10 as function of corpus modality composition (Fused Ratio, Text Ratio) for both Jina-CLIP-v2 and Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B, before (left) and after (right) Trident training. Across all four datasets, the pattern observed in the main text is consistently reproduced. Before training, every surface exhibits pronounced valley concentrated around balanced modality compositions, confirming that the modality preference of baseline retrievers is not an artifact specific to single dataset but rather systematic failure mode that generalizes across document types, ranging from natural images in ChartQA to dense text layouts in DocVQA and ViDoSeek. After Trident training, the valley is consistently eliminated, and Mean NDCG@10 remains stable across the full 25 Figure 14: Distribution of cosine similarities between same-modality and cross-modality positive pairs, ablation studies on Qwen3-VL-E-2B. Figure 15: Effect of explicit modality balancing. Although explicit balancing further reduces modality discrepancy, it does not improve the final retrieval performance. range of Fused Ratio and Text Ratio values. This consistency across datasets with markedly different visual and textual characteristics reinforces our central claim that Trident renders the model insensitive to corpus modality composition, rather than merely overfitting to the modality distribution of particular training or evaluation set. Beyond this overall consistency, closer comparison across the two backbones reveals subtler distinction. For Jina-CLIP-v2, although the pronounced valley is largely flattened after training, the resulting surface is not perfectly uniform: mild fluctuations remain visible, particularly on InfoVQA and DocVQA, where retrieval performance shows slight sensitivity to extreme modality ratios. We attribute this residual variation to the underlying CLIP-based architecture, in which text and image are encoded through separate towers and subsequently aligned only through shared embedding space. Such design inherently treats each modality as distinct representational subspace, so that even after modality-balanced training, complete invariance to corpus composition is difficult to achieve. In contrast, Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B exhibits markedly flatter surface after training, with performance variation across the entire Fused Ratio and Text Ratio grid becoming almost negligible on every dataset. We attribute this difference to the fact that Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B is built upon vision-language model backbone, wherein textual and visual tokens are processed within single unified transformer rather than through separate modality-specific encoders. This architectural unification allows the model to represent text, image, and fused content within shared token space from the outset, providing more favorable inductive bias for eliminating modality preference once explicitly supervised with modality-balanced data. sections.title: I PERFORMANCE ACROSS MATRYOSHKA DIMENSIONS
sections.content: The embedding dimension directly determines the storage and computation cost of retrieval system, and Matryoshka representation learning (Kusupati et al., 2022) allows single model to be used at multiple dimensions. To this end, we incorporate Matryoshka representation learning into the training of Trident (dimensions 1282048) and compare Trident with Qwen3-VL-E-2B in terms of nDCG@10 across embedding dimensions (Figure 17). 27 (a) Performance on Origin Corpus (b) Performance on Mixed-Modality Corpus Figure 17: Performance across Matryoshka embedding dimensions. Origin Corpus. As shown in Figure 17a, Trident performs at least on par with the baseline at every dimension, and its advantage grows as the dimension decreases: the two models are nearly tied at 2048 dimensions (+0.2), while Trident leads by +7.4 at 128 dimensions. This indicates that Trident does not sacrifice unimodal retrieval ability on the original corpus, and better preserves representation quality at low dimensions. Mixed-Modality Corpus. As shown in Figure 17b, Trident outperforms the baseline by large margin at all dimensions (+26.1 to +30.5), and this advantage does not shrink as the dimension increases. The baselines nDCG@10 stays between 33 and 40 throughout, so larger embedding dimension does little to alleviate its degradation on the mixed corpus, whereas Trident at only 128 dimensions already clearly surpasses the baseline at 2048 dimensions. This suggests that Tridents advantage in the mixed-modality setting stems not from greater representational capacity, but from effectively mitigating Modality Preference.
